stem: A subscription-box retailer's web team runs a stateless web tier and must add capacity during flash sales with no downtime and no ceiling imposed by a single instance's size.

choices.text: Update the launch template to a larger instance type and run an instance refresh across the fleet before the sale
Add more instances behind the load balancer through Auto Scaling as demand rises
Increase the Auto Scaling group's maximum capacity, without attaching a scaling policy that would launch new instances as demand rises
Consolidate the fleet onto fewer, larger instances to simplify operations before the sale

rationale: Adding more instances behind the load balancer through Auto Scaling is horizontal scaling: it can happen with no downtime and, because the tier is stateless, has no real ceiling from any single instance's size. Updating the launch template to a larger instance type and running an instance refresh is vertical scaling by replacement: each instance is still stopped and replaced in turn, which is a rolling form of the same brief-outage-per-instance tradeoff, and the fleet is still capped at whatever the new instance type's ceiling is. Raising the Auto Scaling group's maximum capacity without a scaling policy attached does not actually add instances when demand rises; the group has room to grow but nothing tells it to, so capacity stays flat exactly when the flash sale needs it most. Consolidating onto fewer, larger instances reduces the fleet's elasticity and reintroduces the same per-instance ceiling the team is trying to avoid during a demand spike.
